newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hollywood giant to launch DVD movies in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Hollywood giant to launch DVD movies in Japan.

text.p: Hollywood's Warner Home Video said on Monday it plans to start sales in Japan this month of movies on digital video disc (DVD) -- a new format that could make both videos and compact discs obsolete.
The firm said it would be the first commercial launch of movies on the format anywhere in the world and would come well ahead of the planned launch in the United States in early 1997.

An official of Warner Home Video, which is a unit of the giant Time Warner Inc, said the firm would start sales in Japan on December 20 with four major titles, including "Eraser", starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, and "The Fugitive", starring Harrison Ford.
"We will try to increase the number of our DVD software titles every month from now on, but we have no specific target figures at the moment," he said.

Japanese electronics makers such as Toshiba Corp and Matsushita Electric Industrial Co started selling DVD players in Japan on November 1. But a lack of attractive software titles has held back sales.
The Warner move could be a boost for the DVD format as it means movie titles will be on sale in Japan for Christmas.

Another electronics maker announced on Monday it was entering the DVD player market. Akai Electric Co Ltd said it will launch its DVD players in Japan at the end of January and in world markets in April 1997.
Akai said it would be the world's fourth firm to enter the DVD market with originally developed DVD players, following Matsushita, Toshiba and Pioneer Electronic Corp.
The Warner Home Video official said the decision to launch the movie sales in Japan was made following strong representations from Toshiba.
The official said Warner Home Video would probably launch DVD software titles in the United States in March.
A lack of attractive software has forced Toshiba and other major DVD makers to delay the U.S. launch of their products until January or February.
Toshiba has said about 40 to 50 software titles will be available by the time its players hit the U.S. market.

The DVD format is expected to eventually replace video movies, compact discs (CDs) and CD-ROMs. A DVD looks like a CD, but can hold seven to 14 times as much data, allowing it to hold feature-length movies, music and other information.
A single DVD can store movies or albums in several different languages and can be played on a computer or on a home player, much like today's videocassette recorders.
Makers of home electronic equipment see DVDs as a technological leap that will boost slowing sales.
Entertainment firms believe the format will allow them to use film libraries to generate new sales, much like videotaped movies did when they became a mass-market item in the 1980s.

The introduction of movie titles was delayed by tangled negotiations with Hollywood studios on copyright protection. Industry officials finally reached an agreement on copyright protection in October.
